opus-5.5.text:
I'd describe it as optimistic but very early. The basic project is this: we want to be able to take a neural network and find something like an explanation for why it behaves the way it does. Not necessarily a human-understandable explanation, but a kind of heuristic argument, the sort of thing a mathematician might find convincing even when it isn't a proof. For example, "this model outputs this because these internal features correlate in this way." If we could formalize what that kind of argument looks like, then we could ask whether a model's good behavior on the training distribution is explained by the reasons we'd hope for, or whether something else is going on, like the model behaving well because it's being watched.

Most of our work so far has been on the formalization question itself. What does it even mean for an argument to explain a behavior? How do you combine heuristic arguments, and how do you handle it when new considerations overturn an earlier estimate? We've made some real progress. I feel like we understand the shape of the object better than we did a couple of years ago. But we're definitely not at the stage of running this on large models and getting useful answers.

Where I'm most uncertain is whether this is going to work at all. I put maybe a moderate probability on us finding a formal notion of explanation that's both precise enough to be useful and general enough to apply to real learned systems. If it doesn't work, I think we'll learn something about why it's hard, and that's valuable too. If it does work, it could be a pretty big deal for alignment, because it's one of the few approaches I know of that seems to give you leverage on the case where models are actively trying to look good while not actually being good. So that's the bet: a fairly theoretical, somewhat risky research program, with a payoff that I think justifies the risk.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames the potential alignment payoff as conditional and uncertain, and says the work has not yet been run on large models to get useful answers.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses formalizing and combining heuristic arguments, but does not say they use cases simpler than small neural networks to develop the notion of explanation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the basic hope here is that for a lot of the properties of neural networks we care about, there should be some explanation of why the network behaves the way it does, and we'd like a way to find that explanation and then use it to do things like detect anomalous behavior or know when the model is doing something for a reason that's different from the reason it usually does it. The current state is honestly that we've spent a lot of time trying to nail down what we even mean by an explanation, and we're still not there. We have these candidate formalisms, where you say roughly an explanation is a thing that lets you estimate the probability of some behavior, and a good explanation is one that gets the right answer for the right reasons, so it still gives the right answer when you perturb things in ways the explanation says shouldn't matter. But every time we write down a precise version, we find some case where it either accepts a bad explanation or rejects a good one.

So I'd say we're in the stage that's a lot like pre-paradigmatic math or theoretical computer science, where you're trying to find the right definition before you can even state the theorems. That's frustrating, because it's hard to tell from the outside whether you're making progress. The thing I find encouraging is that the failure modes we hit keep getting more interesting and more specific. A year or two ago, the objections were things like, this obviously doesn't handle the simplest possible case. Now the objections are more like, here's a subtle construction where two explanations disagree and it's genuinely unclear which one is correct. That feels like the kind of difficulty you'd expect to hit if the problem were real and tractable, rather than the kind you'd hit if the whole approach were confused.

The other thing I'd say is that we've been trying to be pretty disciplined about building toy cases, like small networks or even just boolean circuits, where we can actually check whether the thing we're calling an explanation does what we want. And a lot of the time it doesn't, which is useful, because it tells you where the definition is wrong. My honest estimate is that there's maybe a reasonable chance this works out into something practically useful, but it's very far from being an applied project. If someone asked me whether this will help with alignment in the next couple of years, I'd say probably not directly. If they asked whether it's one of the more promising long-shot theoretical bets, I'd say yes, that's why I'm spending my time on it.

r001.rationale: The benefits are framed as a “basic hope” and a tentative long-shot, while the work is described as far from applied and focused on unsettled definitions and toy cases rather than demonstrated real-world results.

r002.rationale: The response says they use small networks “or even just boolean circuits” to test what counts as an explanation; boolean circuits are simpler cases than small neural networks.

astra-6.text:
I’d describe it as exploratory. There’s a basic intuition that, if a model does something surprising, we’d like to be able to search for an explanation of why it did that—and then check whether that explanation actually accounts for the behavior. But turning that intuition into a precise research problem is a lot of the work.

The hard part is that an explanation can sound reasonable without telling you what’s really going on. Ideally, it should let you make predictions: if you change this part of the input, or intervene on this part of the computation, what happens? That gives you something to test beyond whether the explanation is persuasive.

I’m interested in whether we can make finding those explanations into a systematic process, with enough structure that we can tell when we’ve succeeded. I think there’s something promising there, but I wouldn’t describe it as a mature approach to alignment yet.

r001.rationale: The response calls the idea exploratory and frames its benefits as an intuition to test, rather than as an empirically established result.

r002.rationale: It does not mention using simpler cases, small neural networks, or any comparable method for developing a notion of explanation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s still pretty early. The basic hope is that, if a model does something, we can search for an explanation of why it did that and then check that explanation more cheaply than we could have found it ourselves. If that worked well enough, it could give us a way to understand and oversee systems that are doing things we couldn’t directly evaluate.

The hard part is specifying what counts as an explanation. You don’t just want a plausible story about the model’s behavior. You want something that actually accounts for the computation, and that lets you distinguish a model doing the thing you intended from one that merely looks good on the examples you checked.

So I’d describe it as a research direction with a lot of conceptual work still to do. I’m interested in whether we can formulate a version of that problem precisely enough that progress on it would tell us something meaningful about alignment.

r001.rationale: The response describes the benefits as a “basic hope” and calls the direction early, but does not clearly say those benefits lack empirical validation.

r002.rationale: It discusses defining an explanation and making the problem precise, but does not mention working it out using cases simpler than small neural networks.
